propositions.text: The claimant alleges he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China and claims refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: XXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, alleges he is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges PRC citizenship and claims refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: In 2007 claimant had chronic stomach problems unrelieved by medical intervention.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that in 2007 he was suffering from chronic stomach problems.

propositions.text: In 2008 claimant began practicing Falun Gong and noticed health improvement.
propositions.quote: In XXX 2008, the claimant was introduced to the practice of Falun Gong as a means to address his health problems. The claimant began practicing at home and noticed an improvement in his health.

propositions.text: In 2008 claimant joined cousin's underground Falun Gong group practice.
propositions.quote: In XXXXXX 2008, the claimant joined his cousin's underground Falun Gong group practice.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges chronic stomach problems in 2007, began Falun Gong in 2008, and joined underground group practice that year.

propositions.text: In 2009 claimant's Falun Gong group was raided; members arrested and detained.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that on XXXXXXX, 2009, the claimant's group practice was raided by members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB). The XXXX members of the group including the claimant were arrested and detained.

propositions.text: Claimant's health deteriorated in custody; released on bail in 2010 with reporting conditions.
propositions.quote: The claimant's stomach ailment returned and his health deteriorated while in custody. On XXXXXX, 2010, the claimant was released on a 10,000 RMB bond so that he could obtain medical treatment with the added conditions that he regularly report to the PSB.

propositions.text: Claimant left China with smuggler's help before returning to detention; PSB issued summons after he failed to report.
propositions.quote: Recognizing that he would soon return to detention, he left China with the assistance of a smuggler and arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2010. The claimant alleges that when he failed to report to the PSB as scheduled, the PSB attended his home to locate him. He further learned that the PSB issued a summons for him.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges Falun Gong group members remain incarcerated.
propositions.quote: He alleges that the members of his Falun Gong group are still being incarcerated.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges his group was raided in 2009, he was detained and released on bail in 2010, fled China, and PSB pursued him with summons.

propositions.text: Claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.

propositions.text: The key issue is claimant's credibility about Falun Gong practice and persecution by Chinese authorities.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's testimony concerning his practice of Falun Gong and his pursuit by authorities in China based on illegal Falun Gong activities.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, claimant is not credible regarding these allegations.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not been a credible witnesses in regard.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the key issue is claimant's credibility about Falun Gong and persecution, and finds claimant not credible on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Claimant established identity as Chinese national with Hukou and Resident Identity Card.
propositions.quote: The claimant established his identity as a national of the People's Republic of China, with his household register booklet or Hukou and Resident Identity Card.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant established his identity as a Chinese national with Hukou and Resident Identity Card.

propositions.text: Panel considered claimant's age, education, background, and English ability in assessing credibility.
propositions.quote: In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education, and background. The claimant alleges he has 9 years of formal education and that he was a XXXXX in China. The panel is also mindful that the claimant testified that he is attending English as a second language classes in Canada and notes that the claimant understood and responded to some of the panel's questions in English and without the aid of translation.

propositions.text: Panel recognized difficulties claimants face including cultural factors, hearing room milieu, interpreter use, and nervousness.
propositions.quote: In addition, the panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter and nervousness.

paragraphs.summary: The panel considered claimant's background, education, English skills, and recognized claimant's difficulties in the hearing when assessing credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges he and six others were arrested and detained for Falun Gong.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he and six other members of his Falun Gong group were arrested and detained.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges temporary release on bail to seek medical attention, then left China for Canada.
propositions.quote: He alleges that he gained temporary release from detention on bail to seek medical attention. He further alleges while on bail he was able to leave China and travel to Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges all group members received multi-year sentences and PSB pursues him.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that all the members of his group received multi-year sentences and that the PSB are in pursuit of him.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges arrest and detention of group, bail release for medical care, fleeing China, and PSB pursuit.

propositions.text: Claimant tendered a summons allegedly left with parents after he failed to report to PSB.
propositions.quote: The claimant tendered into evidence the summons3 that he has alleged was left with his parents after he failed to report to the PSB as directed.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence notes summons usually issued to individual, but often left with family to pass on.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence4 notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or family member. However, it was also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members, instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons.

propositions.text: Person accepting summons expected to sign acknowledgment, though this is improper but common.
propositions.quote: The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. Though this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable

propositions.text: Two types of summons in China: Zuanhuan (non-coercive) and Juzhuan (coercive arrest summons).
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence5 states that there are two types of summonses in China including: Zuanhuan summons is considered a non-coercive measure and is used when no arrest or detention of suspects is contemplated or necessary or when cooperation is expected or flight is not likely; and, Juzhuan summons which is translated as an Arrest-Summon (for Interrogation) summons.

propositions.text: Claimant testified he was arrested, on bail for medical reasons, and PSB intent on arresting him, visiting home 7 times.
propositions.quote: The claimant's testimony is that he had already been arrested but that he was on bail due to medical reasons. He insisted the PSB were intent on arresting him and that they have been to his home on 7 occasions searching for him.

propositions.text: Claimant testified last PSB home visit was in 2011; reasonable to expect PSB would issue coercive Juzhuan summons.
propositions.quote: He testified that they last attended his home in XXXXXX, 2011 in pursuit of him. Given the claimant's allegation that he had previously been incarcerated with the XXXX members of his Falun Gong group and that the police were intent on arresting him, it is reasonable to expect that the PSB would have issued a Juzhuan summons (Arrest-Summon for Interrogation).

paragraphs.summary: Claimant tendered a summons allegedly left with parents; evidence explains summons types and procedures; claimant alleges PSB pursuit and multiple home visits.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence describes summons format: triplicate copies, original at police, duplicate signed and returned, one copy left with suspect or family.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence6 also notes the format and appearance of summonses. It is stated that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect.

propositions.text: Example Juzhuan summons from Fujian Province includes statement about arrest per PRC Criminal Procedure Law Article 45.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence provided an example of the Juzhuan summons from Fujian Province where the claimant is from and notes the information that is to be included on the portion of a summons left with the person or family members of the person named in the summons. It states that the summons should include, among other things, the following statement: According to PRC Criminal Procedure Law Article 45, it has been decided that investigator from this bureau (name) will effectuate arrest at the resident (address) of (named person).

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence describes summons format and example from Fujian Province including legal arrest statement.

propositions.text: Summons tendered lacks claimant's address, date of service, claimant's parents' signature, and required legal statement.
propositions.quote: The summons tendered by the claimant does not contain his address nor is the date of service indicated. The summons also does not bear the signature of the claimant's parents despite his testimony that they were the persons on whom the summons was served. The summons also does not bear the statement "according to PRC Criminal Law Procedure Article 45".

paragraphs.summary: The summons lacks address, service date, parents' signature, and required legal statement.

propositions.text: Summons does not conform to examples; references Security Management Law section 83, not PRC Criminal Procedure Law sections 45 or 92.
propositions.quote: The panel also that the summons tendered by the claimant does not conform to either of the examples of summonses in the country condition documents. In fact, the summons tendered by the claimant bears reference to section 83 of the "Security Management Law of the People's Republic of China rather than sections 45 or 92 of the PRC Criminal Procedure Law.

paragraphs.summary: The summons does not conform to examples and cites incorrect legal provisions.

propositions.text: Summons lacks mention of bail violation; reasonable to expect such mention if claimant failed bail conditions.
propositions.quote: In addition, there is no mention on the summons of the claimant's alleged violation of bail. It is reasonable to expect that given the claimant had failed to honour his bail conditions by failing to report to the PSB that the summons would reflect that in some way.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence notes fraudulent documents including summonses are easily acquired in China.
propositions.quote: The panel notes from the documentary evidence that fraudulent documents including summonses are easily acquired in China.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, summons is not genuine; tendering fraudulent document undermines claimant's credibility.
propositions.quote: I have considered the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant compared to the documentary evidence, as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the summons provided by the claimant is not a genuine document. The panel further finds the tendering of a fraudulent document in support of his claim undermines the claimant overall credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Summons lacks bail violation mention; fraudulent documents are common; summons is likely not genuine, undermining claimant's credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant tendered bail decision letter and bond receipt to corroborate arrest and incarceration.
propositions.quote: The claimant tendered a bail decision letter together with a receipt for payment of his bond as corroboration of his allegation that he had been arrested and incarcerated for his Falun Gong activities.

propositions.text: Receipt indicates payment of fine for illegal Falun Gong, not bond payment; bail letter states bond refundable if conditions met.
propositions.quote: The panel notes that the receipt tendered indicates that the receipt was provided for payment of a fine for illegal Falun Gong activities and not for payment of a bond. The receipt states, "Being Fined for join illegal Falun Gong and Cult." (sic) The bail decision letter makes it clear that the claimant was to be released on bail upon the payment of the 10,000 RMB bond and that the money would not be confiscated unless the claimant failed to comply with the conditions of his bail.

propositions.text: Claimant could not explain discrepancy; documents contradict and are suspect; negative inference drawn.
propositions.quote: The claimant was unable to provide an explanation for the discrepancy. The panel finds that these two documents contradict one another and as such both documents are rendered suspect. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference.

propositions.text: Considering inconsistencies and ease of fraudulent documents, bail letter and receipt are likely not genuine.
propositions.quote: The panel has considered the inconsistencies in the documents provided by the claimant and further considered that the claimant has tendered a fraudulent summons in support of his claim as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the bail decision letter and receipt provided by the claimant are not genuine documents.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant's bail letter and receipt contradict; receipt is a fine, not bond; documents likely not genuine; negative inference drawn.

propositions.text: Claimant used smuggler and false passport to leave China for Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that he used the services of a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada because he was being pursued by the PSB. The claimant alleged that he was provided a false passport by the smuggler.

propositions.text: Claimant did not know details of false passport or identity used during transit.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked what information the smuggler provided him concerning his false identity in the event he was asked questions by officials during transit. The claimant testified that he was only told the name that was in his passport and told to follow the smuggler and not worry. The claimant testified that the passport was written in English and that he could not read the contents. He acknowledged that he did not know if the passport contained his date of birth or it had been previously used by to exit or enter any other countries. The claimant testified that he was posing as a resident of the United Kingdom but stated that he was not provided his fraudulent address in the U.K. The claimant further testified that he did not know the name that the smuggler was using in his passport despite his testimony that they were traveling together and posing as uncle and nephew.

propositions.text: Panel finds it not plausible or credible claimant lacked basic knowledge of false identity during transit.
propositions.quote: While the panel does recognize the need for the Board to be sensitive to the vulnerabilities of claimants traveling under false documents, it does not excuse the claimant for his lack of knowledge of the identity he and the smuggler were traveling under. The panel finds it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would not be aware of this basic information in the face of the obvious likelihood that he would be questioned about it in transit.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant alleges smuggler helped him with false passport but lacked knowledge of identity; panel finds this not credible or plausible.

propositions.text: Claimant's family in China has not suffered consequences from his Falun Gong participation or failure to surrender.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that his family in China has not suffered any consequences as a result of his participation in Falun Gong and failure to surrender to the police.

propositions.text: Country evidence states Falun Gong is banned cult; authorities punish families of absconding practitioners.
propositions.quote: Country documentary evidence7 regarding Falun Gong states that it is considered a cult by the Chinese government and is banned and, indicates that Chinese authorities use the family of absconding practitioners as hostages to force the practitioner to give up the practice. If a practitioner does not cooperate with the authorities, the family is subject to punishment as well, including harassment, arbitrary interrogation, losing a job, and losing housing benefits.

propositions.text: Given seriousness and 18 months absence, reasonable to expect claimant's family would face sanctions; claimant's testimony is minimal threat only.
propositions.quote: The claimant's testimony is that the only "threat" that the family received was they would be punished if they were found to be withholding information about the location of the claimant. In the context of this case, given the seriousness of the accusations, and where the absconding person has not returned for 18 months, and as alleged by the claimant, the PSB are still looking for him as late as XXXXXX of 2011, it is reasonable to assume that his family would have experienced some greater sanctions in an effort to have the claimant turn himself in to the PSB.

propositions.text: Panel draws negative inference from family's normal life without consequences or rigorous interrogation.
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's family continuing ability to carry on with their normal lives without facing consequences or more rigorous interrogation at the hands of the PSB.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant says family not punished; country evidence says families are punished; panel finds family likely would face sanctions and draws negative inference.

propositions.text: Claimant tendered documents to corroborate residency: Resident Identity Card, Hukou, medical records, bail letter and receipt.
propositions.quote: In order to corroborate his residency in China, the claimant tendered a number of original documents, including a Resident Identity Card (RIC), a Household registry (Hukou), medical records as well as his Bail decision letter and receipt.

propositions.text: Documents fail to corroborate residency at material time; RIC and Hukou issued in 2002; bail letter and receipt not genuine.
propositions.quote: However, the panel finds that the documents provided by the claimant fail to provide pervasive corroborative evidence that he resided in China at the time of the alleged raid. The claimant's RIC and his Hukou were issued in 2002 and provide no corroboration that the claimant was living in China after 2002. Having previously found that the bail decision letter and receipt are not genuine documents, they too do not provide corroboration that the claimant was in China at the material time.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant tendered documents to corroborate residency but they fail to prove residency at material time; bail letter and receipt not genuine.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to produce work documents for 2009; explanation of cash payment rejected.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why he had not produced additional work documents to establish his residency in China in 2009. The claimant alleges that no such work records are available because he was paid cash. The panel rejects the claimant's explanation.

propositions.text: Claimant made no effort to obtain work documents despite Board's screening form request and competent counsel.
propositions.quote: The claimant was reminded that he was provided a screening form by the Board which specifically requested that he provide evidence of his work and residency in China. The claimant made no effort to obtain any work documents despite being requested through the screening form. In addition, the claimant is represented by competent counsel and the importance of obtaining these documents is evident.

propositions.text: Claimant alleged 10 years at same company; reasonable to expect some documentation.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the claimant alleges that he worked at the same company for ten years. It is reasonable to expect that he would have some documentation to demonstrate that he worked at the company.

propositions.text: No persuasive evidence corroborates claimant's presence in China at material times; negative inference drawn.
propositions.quote: Unfortunately, as a result, there is no persuasive evidence to corroborate that the claimant was in China at the time he alleges he was being pursued by the PSB. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to obtain work records or other persuasive records to establish he was in China at the material times.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant failed to produce work documents despite requests; panel rejects explanation and draws negative inference on residency.

propositions.text: Claimant tendered two medical booklets from different hospitals covering 2007-2008 and 2010.
propositions.quote: The claimant tendered two medical booklets to corroborate his illness. The medical documents are from two different hospitals. One booklet provides information on the claimant's treatment for his alleged stomach ailment from XXXXXX 2007 to XXXXXX 2008. The second booklet provides information on the treatment of the claimant's stomach ailment from XXXXX 2010 to XXXX 2010.

propositions.text: Medical documents lack other health info, hospital seals, or security features; likely not genuine.
propositions.quote: The panel notes that neither of the documents contains any other information with regard to the health of claimant other than his alleged stomach ailment as would reasonably be expected. Further, the panel notes that neither of the documents contains a hospital chop or seal nor do they contain any security feature to establish their provenance. In addition, I have considered that the claimant has tendered fraudulent documents in support of his claim as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find on a balance of probabilities that the medical booklets provided by the claimant are not genuine documents.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant tendered medical booklets but they lack seals or security features and are likely not genuine.

propositions.text: Based on cumulative negative credibility findings and lack of evidence, claimant's testimony about Falun Gong raid and PSB pursuit is not credible.
propositions.quote: Based on the foregoing cumulative negative credibility findings and negative inferences drawn above, and, the lack of persuasive evidence, the panel finds that the claimant's testimony, that his Falun Group in China was raided and that he is being pursued by the PSB is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's testimony about Falun Gong raid and PSB pursuit not credible due to cumulative negative findings and lack of evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant's understanding of Falun Gong is fairly well developed and he practices in a group in Canada.
propositions.quote: In general, the claimant's understanding of the Falun Gong was fairly well developed. The claimant alleges that while in China he had been practicing Falun Gong in a group once a week and practicing on his own every day. Since being in Canada, the claimant testified that he continues to practice in a group.

propositions.text: Panel gives no weight to claimant's ability to answer questions about Falun Gong.
propositions.quote: As such, the panel gives no weight to the claimant's ability to answer questions about Falun Gong.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant understands Falun Gong well and practices it in Canada but gives no weight to his ability to answer questions about it.

propositions.text: It is necessary to judge the genuineness of the claimant's beliefs in this case.
propositions.quote: While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a claimant's beliefs it is necessary in this case.

propositions.text: Claimant has some knowledge of Falun Gong but that does not prove he is a genuine practitioner.
propositions.quote: Although it is true the claimant does possess some knowledge of Falun Gong it does not necessarily mean he is a genuine practitioner.

propositions.text: Letters from fellow practitioners do not corroborate when claimant began practicing in Canada.
propositions.quote: The claimant provided three letters of support from his fellow practitioners in Canada. However none of the letters corroborate when the claimant began practicing Falun Gong in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant arrived in Canada in 2010 and alleged he began group practice within weeks.
propositions.quote: The claimant arrived in Canada in XXXX 2010 and alleged that he began to practice in a group within weeks.

propositions.text: Two letters state authors met claimant in 2010 while practicing Falun Gong; third letter does not specify when.
propositions.quote: However two of the letters he tendered state that author met the claimant in XXXXX 2010 while practicing Falun Gong. The third letter does not identify when the author first met the claimant.

propositions.text: Claimant's failure to provide corroboration that he resumed group practice shortly after arrival leads to negative inference.
propositions.quote: The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's failure to provide corroboration that he resumed his group practice of Falun Gong shortly after arriving in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's knowledge does not prove genuine practice; letters do not corroborate early practice in Canada; negative inference drawn for lack of corroboration.

propositions.text: Claimant tendered photographs of group Falun Gong activities and demonstrations.
propositions.quote: The claimant also tendered photographs of his participation in group Falun Gong activities including participation in demonstrations XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant testified about his participation and others' remarks about Chinese government treatment of Falun Gong.
propositions.quote: The claimant also testified that he was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant testified that he XXXXXXXXXXXXXX "Falun Gong is good." The claimant further testified that other XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX made disparaging remarks about the Chinese government's treatment of practitioners of Falun Gong.

propositions.text: Panel received a document without translation and thus puts little weight on it.
propositions.quote: The panel was only provided with "XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX however the panel was not provided with a translation of the alleged XXXX. As such, the panel can put little weight on this evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant's photographs and testimony but gives little weight to untranslated evidence.

propositions.text: Documents and testimony only show participation, not motivation.
propositions.quote: these documents and the claimant's testimony can only attest to the claimant's participation in Falun Gong activities; they do not attest to his motivation.

propositions.text: Pastor's assessment of faith genuineness cannot substitute panel's assessment.
propositions.quote: recent case law8 indicates that a pastor's assessment of the genuineness of a person's faith cannot be substituted for the assessment that the panel is required to make.

propositions.text: Similarly, a Falun Gong practitioner's assessment cannot substitute the panel's assessment.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the assessment a Falun Gong practitioner cannot be substituted for the assessment the panel is required to make.

propositions.text: Panel gives little evidentiary weight to these documents.
propositions.quote: The panel gives little evidentiary weight to these documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds participation evidence does not show motivation; panel must assess genuineness, not others; little weight given to documents.

propositions.text: Some photographs show claimant joining a demonstration in Toronto.
propositions.quote: some of the photographs tendered by the claimant are of the claimant joining a demonstration XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Toronto.

propositions.text: Claimant testified he is more at risk since a certain time because Chinese authorities will identify him.
propositions.quote: the claimant testified that since XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX he is more at risk because the Chinese authorities will identify him.

propositions.text: Claimant testified he believed the 'Master' would protect him and his parents despite risks of demonstrating.
propositions.quote: The claimant responded that he believed it was the right thing to do and that he did not think it was a risk because the "Master would protect" him.

propositions.text: Panel rejects claimant's testimony about protection by the 'Master'.
propositions.quote: The panel rejects the claimant's testimony.

propositions.text: Claimant practiced Falun Gong secretly in China to avoid PSB, contradicting belief in protection.
propositions.quote: The claimant had the opportunity in China to practice Falun Gong openly as means of protest against the Chinese government's treatment of Falun Gong, however, he chose to practice in secret to avoid the repercussion of the PSB.

propositions.text: Claimant's actions in China undermine his testimony about protection by the 'Master'.
propositions.quote: The claimant's actions in China tend to undermine his testimony that the "Master" would protect him.

propositions.text: Panel finds it unreasonable claimant would risk further endangering himself and family by demonstrating in Canada.
propositions.quote: the panel finds it unreasonable that he would create circumstances which would further endanger him and his family.

propositions.text: Panel draws a negative inference from claimant's risk-taking demonstration in Canada.
propositions.quote: In this regard the panel draws a negative inference.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's risk-taking demonstration testimony rejected; his secret practice in China contradicts belief in protection; negative inference drawn.

propositions.text: Claimant's Falun Gong group practice was not raided and he is not pursued by PSB.
propositions.quote: Having previously found that the claimant's Falun Gong group practice was not raided and that he is not being pursued by the PSB

propositions.text: Claimant was not a genuine practitioner in China as alleged.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant was not a genuine practitioner in China as he alleges.

propositions.text: Claimant's allegation of genuine practice in China is not credible and was to support a fraudulent claim.
propositions.quote: the claimant's allegation that he was a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China is not credible and was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant was not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in China and his claim was fraudulent.

propositions.text: Panel must consider if claimant is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in Canada after finding he was not in China.
propositions.quote: Having found that the claimant was not a Falun Gong practitioner in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner in this county.

propositions.text: Good faith is reasonable to expect in making a refugee claim, especially sur place claims.
propositions.quote: the panel finds it reasonable to expect 'good faith' in making a refugee claim.

propositions.text: Refugee Status Appeals Authority stated no good faith requirement in sur place claims allows appellant to unilaterally determine refugee status grant.
propositions.quote: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it must consider claimant's good faith in Canada; good faith is required in refugee claims, especially sur place claims.

propositions.text: Hathaway's law states manipulating circumstances to create persecution chance is not genuine sur place claim.
propositions.quote: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution which did not exist cannot be said to belong to this category.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant deliberately created circumstances to increase persecution risk and claim not made in good faith.
propositions.quote: The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant deliberately created circumstances to increase his jeopardy of persecution. As such, the panel finds on a balance of probability, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant deliberately created persecution risk and did not make claim in good faith, citing Hathaway's law.

propositions.text: Claimant began Falun Gong activities in Canada only to support a fraudulent refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that the claimant began Falun Gong activities in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant began Falun Gong activities in Canada solely to support a fraudulent claim.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner nor would he be perceived as such in China.
propositions.quote: the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner nor would he be perceived to be in China.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner and would not be perceived as one in China.

propositions.text: Claimant has not established serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment in China.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to prove serious risk of persecution or cruel treatment in China.

propositions.text: Claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection; claim rejected.
propositions.quote: The claimant is neither Convention refugees nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant is not a refugee or person in need of protection and rejects the claim.
